confidence_why: Pompino-Marschall, Steriopolo and Żygis (2017), Pugh and Press (1999), De Bray (1969), Steriade and Yanovich (2015) and the acoustic studies of Łukaszewicz and Mołczanow (2018-2024) all describe Ukrainian main stress as free and lexically determined, falling on any syllable and shifting within paradigms; they differ only on secondary stress and on a penultimate tendency, and a fixed penultimate pattern is reported only for some Western dialects.

catalog_quote: Word stress is free in Ukrainian (Brovčenko 1969). It can be contrastive: ˈkury [ˈkurɪ] 'chicken' (pl) vs. kuˈry [kuˈrɪ] 'to smoke' or doˈroha [dɔˈrɔɦa] 'road' vs. doroˈha [dɔrɔˈɦa] 'dear'. The main stress can appear on any syllable in a given word, e.g. ˈvy-ra-xu-va-nyj [ˈʋɪraxuʋanɪj] 'calculated', za-ˈlja-ku-va-ty [zaˈlʲakuʋatɪ] 'to intimidate', po-vi-ˈdo-my-ty [pɔʋʲiˈdɔmɪtɪ] 'to inform', pry-sto-su-ˈva-nec' [prɪstɔsuˈʋanɛtsʲ] 'conformist', pe-re-po-vi-ˈsty [pɛrɛpɔʋʲiˈstɪ] 'to relate' (Danylenko & Vakulenko 1995: 13). The stress can also move within a paradigm: ro-ˈby-ty [rɔˈbɪtɪ] 'to do', ro-ˈblju [rɔˈblʲu] 'I do', ˈro-byš [ˈrɔbɪʃ] 'you do' (de Bray 1951: 74). It is sensitive to morphology and its shifting nature reinforces the distinctive function of morphological constituents; for a historical background of the 'morphologization' of stress see Shevelov (1979: 120–126). sweep_summary: Two title hits for Ukrainian (ukra1253, catalog classification lexical, deciding source Pompino-Marschall et al. 2017 JIPA). (1) Yanovich & Steriade 2010 is an unpublished OCP talk with no open text found; its published successor, Steriade & Yanovich 2015 'Accentual allomorphs in East Slavic' (Equinox, 60-page chapter), is open on Steriade's MIT page and was downloaded and read: stress position in Ukrainian is 'in principle unconstrained' with four lexical accentual noun classes, plus a preference for penultimate stress in standard Ukrainian (invariant penult reported for some Western dialects) — confirms and refines the catalog's lexical coding; does not supersede the JIPA illustration as deciding source. (2) Al'muhamedova & Kul'sharipova 1980 is about Russian o-kanje dialects; Glottolog's Ukrainian link is a flagged computerized misassignment from 'slova' — irrelevant, priority none. Saved:, and updated. Semantic Scholar, OpenAlex, archive.

new_statements.quote: The East Slavic accentual systems have a shared characteristic: the position of the stress is in principle unconstrained. In Ukrainian, however, penultimate stress is preferred. In some Western Ukrainian dialects, this preference is reported as an invariant fact (Zilynskyj 1979: 184, 194; Reiter 1969; Baerman 1999). The data we analyse – from standard Ukrainian, based on Eastern dialect – show that aspects of the penult preference are present in general.

new_statements.reading: Ukrainian word stress is lexically determined (position 'in principle unconstrained'; nouns belong to four lexically indexed accentual classes with fixed-stem, post-accenting and mobile patterns), overlaid with a statistical/markedness preference for penultimate main stress in standard (Eastern) Ukrainian and a reported fixed: penultimate syllable pattern in some Western dialects. This confirms the catalog's 'lexical' coding and refines it by naming the penult bias (450 penult vs 370 final vs 55 antepenult among database base nouns).

Furthermore, a subtle increase in duration of the word-final vowel serves as a cue for rhythmic stress in Ukrainian.

new_statements.relation_note: Agrees with the catalog/Steriade & Yanovich reading that primary stress is lexical and unpredictable; adds that there is a predictable rhythmic secondary-stress layer (hybrid system) and that duration, extending to the pretonic syllable, is the acoustic cue. Abstract only: the CC-BY ScienceDirect PDF could not be reached by automated download bot-block pages on both automated download attempts; Unpaywall/Semantic Scholar list no other open copy except the UW repository item/123447, whose DSpace record exposes no bitstreams to anonymous users.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary (lexical) stress is unpredictable and must be learned per word; on top of it there is predictable rhythmic (secondary) stress, so the authors call the system 'hybrid (lexical-grammatical)'. Duration is the main cue: the lexically stressed vowel is long (the lengthening reaches the pretonic syllable) and the word-final vowel is slightly lengthened as a rhythmic-stress cue.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Yes: 'rhythmic (predictable) stress' in addition to lexical stress; the abstract's test words are of the shapes σˈσσˌσ / ˌσσˈσσ, i.e. a rhythmic secondary stress two syllables from the primary one, with a duration cue on the word-final vowel.
new_statements.identity_note: All three works describe standard modern Ukrainian; Pugh & Press say explicitly that the grammar describes 'the standard language'. The instrumental studies report on native speakers (14 speakers in Mołczanow et al. 2021) without a dialect specification in the abstracts. No work addresses the Western Ukrainian fixed: penultimate syllable dialects mentioned in the existing Steriade & Yanovich statement.

new_statements.quote: Recent work suggests that Ukrainian represents a typologically rare bidirectional stress system with internal lapses, i.e. sequences of unstressed syllables in the vicinity of primary stress (Łukaszewicz and Mołczanow 2018a, b). [...] it involves interaction between free lexical stress and secondary stresses. [...] It focuses on words with primary stress on the fifth syllable. Such words are predicted to have secondary stress on the first and third syllables. The results point to statistically significant lengthening of vowels carrying lexical stress as well as of those in the initial syllable, but not in the third syllable.

new_statements.relation_note: Same primary-stress type as the catalog/existing statement ('free lexical stress'); adds the secondary-stress system (bidirectional, initial secondary stress) and its acoustic correlates. Abstract only: the open_url is a DSpace landing page whose REST API returns zero bundles/bitstreams for the record (ClosedAccess icon), so the 'open copy' is metadata only; the De Gruyter DOI page returned HTTP 202 with an empty body (bot challenge).
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress is free (lexical); secondary stresses are assigned rhythmically from the word edge in a bidirectional pattern (e.g. a word with primary stress on syllable 5 is expected to carry secondary stress on syllables 1 and 3), with lapses (runs of unstressed syllables) allowed next to the primary stress. Acoustically, the lexically stressed vowel and the initial-syllable vowel are significantly lengthened; the predicted third-syllable secondary stress did not show vowel lengthening.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Yes: bidirectional rhythmic secondary stress, with an initial-syllable secondary stress confirmed by vowel lengthening and a word-internal one (syllable 3) not confirmed by vowel parameters; the authors suggest consonant duration may carry word-internal subsidiary stress.

new_statements.relation_note: Agrees with the catalog's lexical coding and with Steriade & Yanovich 2015 (position 'in principle unconstrained', nouns in lexically indexed accentual classes with fixed, post-accenting and mobile patterns). It does not mention the penult preference. On secondary stress it differs in emphasis from the Łukaszewicz-Mołczanow instrumental work: Pugh & Press restrict secondary stress to compounds, whereas the 2018/2021 abstracts report rhythmic secondary stress in ordinary polysyllabic words.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is free and lexically determined ('no general rule as to where the stress falls'); it is also mobile within paradigms for many words. Stress is contrastive (minimal pairs such as за́мок 'castle' vs замо́к 'lock', о́бід 'hoop' vs обі́д 'lunch', p. 24). Nouns are classified by stress pattern (SS stem-stress throughout, SE stem in sg./ending in pl., EE ending throughout, ES ending in sg./stem in pl., with '+' for further shifts, p. 59); in Conjugation II -и- verbs 'stress is generally not stable, but will shift in the non-past in most verbs when stress is on -и́-ти; stress is stable in the past' (p. 221).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Secondary stress is marked with a grave accent and is 'restricted to compound words' (p. 24).
new_statements.exceptions: Stress mobility across paradigms; a modern tendency to move stress onto the plural endings in first-declension a-stem nouns of three or more syllables (ма́ківка - маківки́), occasionally in disyllables (ху́стка, кни́жка, ді́вка, рі́чка), p. 25; special stress rules for nouns after the numerals two, three, four (p. 59); variation where two stresses are given.
new_statements.identity_note: All three works describe standard modern Ukrainian; Pugh & Press say explicitly that the grammar describes 'the standard language'. The instrumental studies report on native speakers (14 speakers in Mołczanow et al. 2021) without a dialect specification in the abstracts. No work addresses the Western Ukrainian fixed: penultimate syllable dialects mentioned in the existing Steriade & Yanovich statement.

readall_conflicts: No source disagrees on the type of primary stress: Pugh & Press (1999: 25) state there is no general rule for where stress falls and that it must be learned word by word, and the two Łukaszewicz-Mołczanow abstracts call it 'free lexical stress' / 'lexical (unpredictable) stress', matching the existing Steriade & Yanovich 2015 statement. The one difference concerns secondary stress: Pugh & Press (p. 24) say secondary stress is 'restricted to compound words', while the 2018 and 2021 instrumental studies (abstracts only) describe a predictable rhythmic secondary-stress layer in non-compound polysyllables (bidirectional, initial-syllable secondary stress confirmed by vowel lengthening; word-final duration cue for rhythmic stress). This is a descriptive-orthographic statement versus an acoustic-phonetic claim rather than a contradiction about placement of primary stress. Pugh & Press mention a tendency to shift stress to plural endings in longer a-stem nouns, which is compatible with, but not the same as, the penult preference reported by Steriade & Yanovich.

sources.quote: 'Ukrainian has lexical primary stress and predictable rhythmic stress. Lexical stress can appear in any syllable of the word ... The most salient cue to primary stress is duration.' Traditional sources report subsidiary stress; 'rhythmic stresses are placed at both word edges, with additional rhythmic beats intervening between the primary and the secondary stresses, e.g. velosypedýst [ˌʋɛlɔˌsɨpɛˈdɨst]'. Pilot acoustic study (4 speakers, segmentally identical pairs popádaty/popadáty) finds duration differences depending on presence vs absence of (rhythmic) stress.
